topic.title: I/O virtualization
topic.para: In addition to CPU and memory, &vmguest;s share the &vmhost;'s physical I/O subsystems such as network interfaces, storage controllers and GPUs. Because purely software-based I/O introduces latency and CPU overhead, &productname; provides a choice of I/O virtualization techniques that trade off hardware compatibility against near-native performance:

listitem.para: The &vmhost; emulates well-known, legacy physical hardware, such as an Intel e1000 network adapter or an IDE/SATA disk controller. Because the virtualized device behaves identically to real hardware, the &vmguest; can use its built-in operating system drivers without modification. However, every I/O operation must be intercepted and translated by the &vmhost;, causing significant CPU overhead and higher latency. Device emulation is primarily used for booting legacy operating systems or during initial OS installation before paravirtualized drivers are loaded.

Instead of emulating physical hardware, paravirtualized I/O exposes a standardized, hypervisor-aware virtual device interface (virtio) directly to the &vmguest;. The guest OS uses virtio drivers (included in Linux and available for Windows) to communicate efficiently with the &vmhost; via shared memory ring buffers. Combining virtio with kernel-space or user-space offloading (vhost/vhost-user) eliminates costly context switches, delivering high throughput and low latency while preserving live migration and full hardware independence.

Virtual Function I/O (VFIO) assigns an entire physical &vmhost; device (such as a PCIe NVMe drive, NIC or GPU) directly to a single &vmguest;. Using the hardware IOMMU, VFIO isolates device memory access and allows the &vmguest;'s native vendor driver to interact directly with the hardware, completely bypassing the &vmhost; I/O stack. While VFIO delivers near-native performance, a passed-through device cannot be shared with the &vmhost; or other &vmguest;s, and live migration is generally unsupported.

SR-IOV is a PCIe hardware standard that allows a single physical device to partition itself into multiple lightweight Virtual Functions (VFs). Each VF appears as an independent PCIe device that can be assigned directly to a separate &vmguest; via VFIO. SR-IOV combines the near-native performance of direct device assignment with the ability to share a single physical device across multiple &vmguest;s. SR-IOV requires explicit support from the PCIe device, CPU/chipset, BIOS/EFI and host kernel.

For devices that lack SR-IOV hardware partitioning, such as certain enterprise GPUs, the Linux mediated device framework allows a &vmhost; driver to split a single physical device into multiple software-defined virtual devices exposed through VFIO.

important.title: Requirements for VFIO and SR-IOV
important.para: To be able to use the VFIO and SR-IOV features, the &vmhost; needs to fulfill the following requirements:

listitem.para: IOMMU needs to be enabled in the BIOS/EFI.
For Intel CPUs, the kernel parameter intel_iommu=on needs to be provided on the kernel command line.
The vfio_pci kernel module needs to be loaded.
